name: hard-conversation
summary: The speaker keeps putting off calling their brother to ask him to take two days a week of their mother's care, and works out that the real fear is not a no but a quiet yes that never turns into action. They land on asking for the days first, keeping a paid helper as the fallback, telling him about the work strain, and calling Saturday morning. Labels: deepen where they say his silence is worse than a fight, which is worth opening up; leave on the long silence after they name the fear of a hollow yes; decide where they weigh asking for time against asking for money; finished on the plan to call before ten.

utterances.text: So I've been meaning to call Danny for, I think it's three weeks now
and every time I get to the point of actually dialing I find something else to do,
like last night I reorganized the spice drawer, which is, that's where I'm at.
The thing I want to say is pretty simple when I write it down.
I need him to take two days a week with Mom.
Not every other weekend, not when he can, two actual days, Tuesday and Thursday would be ideal
because that's when her PT is and that's when I've been leaving work early.
And I've left early something like, um, eleven times since January
and my manager hasn't said anything yet but she's going to.
And what I'm afraid of, I mean, there's a few versions.
The first one is he says you chose to live ten minutes from her,
which is true, I did, I moved back in twenty nineteen and he didn't,
and so somehow that makes it my job, like I signed up for it by signing a lease.
And the second one is worse honestly, which is he doesn't argue at all,
he just goes quiet and says yeah okay, and then nothing changes
and I'm the one who has to bring it up again in two months and be the, the nag.
utterances.label: deepen
utterances.note: They call the quiet agreement worse than an argument but haven't said why yet.

utterances.text: Because when he argues at least I know where he is.
When he goes quiet I'm basically talking to, to a wall that agrees with me.
And that's what happened with the house stuff after Dad died, um, he said he'd handle the paperwork with the county
and eight months later I was the one sitting in that office with the folder.
So maybe that's actually the thing I'm scared of.
Not that he says no, that he says yes and I have to believe it.
utterances.label: leave
utterances.note: They have just named the real fear and are sitting with it.

utterances.text: Okay. I think, I think part of why I keep putting it off is I haven't decided what I do if he does say no.
Like is there a version where I say fine and I hire someone for those two days,
it's about forty dollars an hour around here, so that's, uh, three hundred and twenty a week if it's four hours each,
and I ask him to split it.
Which honestly might be easier for him, writing a check, he's always been better at the check than the showing up.
But I don't want it to just be money either.
Mom asks about him. She asked on Sunday when Daniel's coming and I said soon,
and I don't know if soon is true.
So the money thing solves my calendar and doesn't solve that.
utterances.label: decide
utterances.note: They are weighing asking for his time against asking for his money.

utterances.text: I think I ask for the days first. Ask for the days, and the money is the fallback, I don't lead with it
because if I lead with it he'll take it, he'll take the easy one.
And I want to say the part about work too, not as a guilt thing, just, um, as a fact
that I can't keep doing eleven early days a quarter and keep the job.
He doesn't know that. I've never told him that, I've kind of made it look fine,
which is maybe partly on me, if I'm being fair.
I'm going to call him Saturday morning, he's usually out running errands and more relaxed then,
not text, because if I text he'll answer in a week with a thumbs up.
Saturday, before ten.
utterances.label: finished
utterances.note: They have set a time to make the call, and the thought is complete.
